storm.summary_layperson: No storm is currently tracking toward the cove — the nearest cell, 34 miles west, is drifting away — but the atmosphere is unstable enough this evening that new thunderstorms are possible nearby, and the Sound's cooling effect here is only moderate, not strong enough to promise real protection if one develops closer.
storm.local_effect_blurb: A real but modest marine layer is in place — 8.3°F air-water gap now, still projected around 5.4°F by 7 PM — but that falls short of the >10°F gap the model requires to call the Sound's cooling a reliably active shield, so no mitigation credit tonight.
storm.detail_html:
NWS OKX's afternoon discussion flags isolated strong to severe thunderstorms with heavy downpours as possible this afternoon/evening as the atmosphere destabilizes, with CAMs agreeing on roughly 2000 J/kg of instability nearby — the fetched HRRR run reads 2270 J/kg locally with strong 0-6 km shear (36-44 kt), a combination that favors organized, potentially strong cells rather than garden-variety showers.

Radar (KOKX, scanned 3:47 PM EDT) shows one cell of note: 34 miles west at 38 dBZ, currently moving away from the cove at about 5 kt toward the southwest. Nothing is presently closing on Greenwich Cove, so there's no arrival window to publish right now.

The Sound's stabilizing setup is real but middling: water is 74.1°F against 82.4°F air, an 8.3°F gap. That's enough for a moderate marine layer and a "high" geometric likelihood that any cell crossing the Sound loses some steam — but the model's bar for calling the mechanism reliably active is a >10°F gap, which this doesn't clear. Projected forward, the gap actually holds up fairly well through the evening (8.3°F now, 5.4°F by 7 PM, staying above the 5°F collapse threshold throughout the available forecast), so there's a real if partial buffer for anything that does develop and track this way later.

No sea breeze is running today (only 25% of coastal stations show a southerly component, below the threshold), so the amplifying punch-through-plus-convergence scenario isn't in play either. Net call for tonight: moderate risk from a broadly unstable regional airmass, with the cove getting a partial — not decisive — discount versus locations further inland if a new cell tracks in off the Sound.

What would change the call: a new cell developing on a westerly-to-northwesterly track toward the cove would need to be watched closely given the shear/CAPE combination; the AFD also flags a second, more organized round arriving late tonight into early Friday, which is beyond this run's model horizon.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind (2-4 kt) backing from SSE early to NE by dark, with no sea breeze in play — early SSE-SE flow leaves the east shore sheltered by Tod's Point, so favor the west/right side, but expect it to go essentially calm and wandering by dusk.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only, light-wind day — no sea breeze in the mix. The land-sea temperature gap (8.3°F) does clear the thermal-window gate, but only 25% of coastal stations show any southerly component, well short of what's needed to call a sea breeze running. Direction agreement across the station network is just 0.5, reflecting a genuinely unsettled regional pattern rather than a coherent single flow.

RYC (ground truth for the cove) is reading SSE 157° at 2.2 kt, gusting to 5.4 — a close match to HRRR's own near-term forecast of SSE 156°. The broader network is messier: KBDR and KHPN read WNW, the multi-station ensemble median is SW 234°, and NWS's generic point forecast calls for a 7 mph W wind — none of it agrees closely with the cove's live read or with each other, which is itself the story: genuinely light, directionless gradient flow with scattered instability nearby scrambling the signal. Trusting the live cove observation and near-term HRRR over the generic NWS text and the broader ensemble average.

HRRR's own forecast backs steadily hour over hour — 156° to 124° to 45° — while speed falls from 3.6 to 1.7 kt, arriving at near-calm right around the thermal-collapse/sunset window (6:53 / 7:23 PM). There was no real thermal running today to begin with, so "collapse" here just means the gradient flow itself dying out. HRRR has no data past 7 PM tonight (f05-f12 unavailable), so the 8-10 PM read is a persistence estimate off the last modeled hour, not fresh model output — treat it as low confidence. With CAPE at 2270 J/kg and strong shear in the area, any nearby cell that fires could throw a brief, erratic outflow gust through the cove that overrides this light ambient flow without warning.

Geography: with the early wind out of SSE-SE, Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) partially shelters the east side of the course — expect the lightest, shiftiest air on the east shore and steadier (if still light) pressure on the west side. Favor the west/right side early. By the time it backs to NE it would normally be the cleanest, most laminar direction in the cove, but at near-calm speed there isn't enough pressure anywhere to really exploit that character.

2-4 kt easing toward calm is drifter territory — expect a patient, shifty race with starts getting progressively lighter through the window, and don't be surprised if the last start of the evening sees the wind essentially die.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast data available only through ~7:00 PM EDT (f01-f04); 8 additional forecast hours (f05-f12) failed to fetch/parse — the 20:00-22:00 wind values are trend-based estimates, not fresh model output.

HRRR's near-term forecast direction (SSE/SE) matches live RYC obs closely, but diverges ~29° from the broader station ensemble (median SW) and NWS's generic point forecast (W) — cove-specific obs and near-term HRRR trusted over both.
Buoy 44040 / WLIS_MET ERDDAP fetch failed (404) — no direct over-water sea-breeze depth signal; relying on the APRS coastal cluster and RYC instead.
No cell is currently closing on the cove (nearest tracked cell, 34 mi W, is moving away), so no storm arrival window is published this run.
